paragraphs.text: This oolong was grown in [Taiwan](taiwan:where-it-is), the island across the strait from Fujian, where most tea gardens lie on the western side of the central range, sheltered from ocean storms. The record names only the island, not a mountain or township, so the [origin tells you](taiwan:on-a-label) where the leaf grew and nothing more about its height or district.

It is an [oolong](oolong:definition), the partly oxidised tea that stands between green and red, and it was rolled, the form most of the [island's oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) takes. Both the plants and the craft came over with settlers from Fujian. From the 1860s this oolong was sold abroad as [Formosa Oolong](taiwan-oolong:history), and in the late twentieth century more of it stayed on the island to be drunk at home.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.

unsupported.why: The claim says Taiwan oolong in general was sold abroad as Formosa Oolong from the 1860s. Saying "this oolong" pins that history on this particular tea, Buddha Palm, and nothing in the record or the claims says Buddha Palm was part of that trade.
